citation: van der Meer, Nesse, Vivian van der Werf, Willem-Paul Brinkman & Marcus Specht. "Virtual Reality and Collaborative Learning: A Systematic Literature Review." Frontiers in Virtual Reality 4 (2023): 1159905. https://doi.org/10.3389/frvir.2023.1159905.
discipline: Educational technology / computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) — PRISMA systematic review
thesis: As the first systematic (PRISMA) review specific to Virtual Reality for Collaborative Learning (VRCL), this article establishes, across 139 empirical studies, that the field is dominated by non-HMD, monitor-based VR with general-purpose controls rather than HMD VR; identifies five skill categories trained, nine required VRCL design features, and five affordances (engagement, remote collaboration, multi-/interdisciplinary spaces, social-skill development, fit with CL pedagogies); and concludes with general literature optimism tempered by an acknowledged absence of clearly established VRCL pedagogy.

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Frames VRCL as an outgrowth of CSCL (since the 1980s) grounded in social-learning theory. Surveys three prior VRCL reviews (Muhammad Nur Affendy & Ajune Wanis 2019; Zheng et al. 2019; Scavarelli et al. 2021) as jointly establishing general optimism, five prior-identified affordances, and four gaps (accessibility, VE-real-world interplay, pedagogical strategy, real-vs-novel-situation balance). States four research questions on skills/competences, domains/disciplines, systems, and empirical knowledge.

sections.title: 2. Methods
sections.summary: Scopus + Web of Science search string (collaboration x VR/AR/MR/XR x empirical-data x education x system terms); 1,608 unique records after de-duplication; five inclusion / seven exclusion criteria narrow this to 139 articles via PRISMA screening. Reliability: five additional coders on a 50-study sample (Cohen's kappa=0.77); a three-category taxonomy (Education/System/Evaluation, partly built on Bloom 1956) applied and checked against a second coder on 30 studies (kappa=0.60, 85% agreement).

sections.title: 3. Descriptive results
sections.summary: Education dimension: 64.0% tertiary education; scaffolding (55.4%) dominant educator role; synchronous collaboration (62.6%); constructivism (33.1%) and PBL (41.0%) dominant paradigms; cognitive-domain outcomes (50.4%) far outweigh affective (7.9%) and psychomotor (5.0%). System dimension: 78.4% non-HMD 3D simulation vs 7.2% HMD VR; 89.2% flat-surface monitor/display hardware; 79.9% general-purpose controls vs 11.5% positional tracking; 67.6% full-body embodiment; small groups (37.4%) and pairs (22.3%) modal sizes. Evaluation dimension: self-report dominant (85.6%) over behavioral (59.0%) and physiological (0.7%, one study); pre-experimental designs dominant (79.9%) over true-experimental (5.8%); 53.2% of studies sampled 1-25 participants; outcomes skew strongly positive (70.5% positive-or-better vs 2.2% negative).

sections.title: 4. Qualitative results
sections.summary: Elaborates five skill categories (cultural, domain-specific, learning, physical, social — Table 4) and nine VRCL design features (embodiment, communication tools, usability/accessibility, perceived usefulness/social presence, object-interaction, equal-input task design, educator support, learner autonomy, socialization-support). Discusses low HMD representation (cost, cybersickness, missing pedagogy, weak empirical base) against contrasting evidence (Makransky & Lilleholt 2018 for HMD arousal/motivation advantage; Makransky et al. 2019 and Parong & Mayer 2021 for HMD distraction/poorer-learning findings). Adopts Girvan's (2018) VE/VR definitions to argue the five affordances belong to the VRCL environment, not the access tool, while conceding tool choice still moderates outcomes. Restates the five VRCL affordances with supporting citations (de Back et al. 2020 on CAVE-based collaborative learning; Molka-Danielsen & Brask 2014 on presence/awareness/belonging).

sections.title: 5. Conclusion and future research
sections.summary: Restates the five skill categories, nine design features, and low HMD representation; reiterates general optimism tempered by lacking pedagogy. Proposes four future-research directions: systematic HMD-vs-non-HMD comparison, more affective/psychomotor attention, more true-experimental designs, adoption of physiological measures (near-absent at 0.7%).

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: used only glancingly — two mentions total (p.9, p.11), both citing VRCL-specific sources (Edirisingha et al. 2009; Denoyelles & Kyeong-Ju Seo 2012), not the CMC-tradition canon; never defined or measured by the review's own taxonomy. The review prefers broader terms (collaboration, socialization, awareness/belonging) as its actual working vocabulary.

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: invoked generally as VR's capacity to make users behave as in the physical world (citing Jensen & Konradsen 2018); listed as a contributor to VRCL affordance #1 (social interaction, strengthened by immersion and presence)

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: the review's central taxonomic axis is 'degree of virtuality' (AR/MR vs 3D-simulation-non-HMD vs HMD VR); operationalized as a hardware category, not a phenomenological construct; 78.4% non-HMD, 16.5% AR/MR, 7.2% HMD

constructs.label: embodiment / self-representation
constructs.treatment: coded as 'type of virtual embodiment' (none/tools/partial/full-body); full-body dominant (67.6%), largely a default of Second Life/OpenSimulator avatar systems

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: coded as 'student engagement' learning goal (31.7% of studies); named as VRCL affordance #1 ('efficient tool to engage and motivate learners')

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: folded into 'cognitive domain' learning-goal category (50.4%); knowledge-transfer discussed narratively via Carron et al. (2013)

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: the review's own primary RQ1 taxonomy: five skill categories (cultural, domain-specific, learning, physical, social) with worked examples

readings.claim: VRCL is an outgrowth of CSCL (since the 1980s), itself grounded in social-learning theory concerning acquisition of behavior through observation.
Systems used for VRCL predominantly implement non-HMD, monitor-based VR with mouse-and-keyboard controls, contrasting what VR is commonly associated with (HMD, specialized controls).

Four candidate explanations for low HMD representation: cost; accessibility burden in multi-person settings; cybersickness risk; and persistent lack of established HMD pedagogy plus weak empirical evidence of educational value.

Following Girvan (2018), VRCL's affordances belong to the virtual environment, not the access tool — but tool choice still moderates outcomes (HMD: higher embodiment/arousal/motivation per Makransky & Lilleholt 2018; non-HMD: fewer distractions per Makransky et al. 2019, Parong & Mayer 2021).

Whether HMD VR is a benefit or a burden depends on three elements: the goals (skills targeted), the setting (discipline/field), and which VRCL affordances matter most for those goals — a deliberately conditional, non-adjudicating conclusion.

Five affordances of VRCL: (1) efficient engagement/motivation tool, (2) support for distance learning/remote collaboration via heightened 'immediacy', (3) multi-/interdisciplinary learning spaces, (4) social-skill development via social presence/socialization, (5) fit with CL pedagogical paradigms.
General literature optimism (70% positive/promising-or-better outcomes) is tempered by a lack of clearly structured, established VRCL pedagogy.
Future research should pursue systematic HMD-vs-non-HMD comparison, more affective/psychomotor attention, more true-experimental designs, and adoption of physiological measures.

concepts.term: five skill categories (cultural, domain-specific, learning, physical, social)

interlocutors.name: De Back, Tinga, Nguyen & Louwerse (2020) — ped-sec-33 companion paper
interlocutors.role: directly cited (p.14 reference list; §4.4) for CAVE-based immersive collaborative learning benefits — almost certainly the companion paper to this cluster's ped-sec-33

interlocutors.name: Makransky et al. (2019) — ped-sec-10
interlocutors.role: cited for HMD VR causing affective/cognitive overloads and distraction, leading to poorer learning outcomes than non-HMD

interlocutors.name: Parong & Mayer (2021) — ped-sec-13
interlocutors.role: cited for HMD VR causing high affective and cognitive distractions, echoing Makransky et al.'s finding

interlocutors.name: Radianti et al. (2020) — ped-sec-22
interlocutors.role: cited (with Sousa Santos et al. 2009 and Makransky et al. 2019) for HMD VR's continued lack of empirical evidence of educational value

interlocutors.name: Dalgarno & Lee (cited as 2010) — ped-sec-04
interlocutors.role: cited early for VR's spatial-learning affordance, alongside de Back et al. (2020); dated 2010 in this article's reference list = the version-of-record year the cluster now adopts for ped-sec-04, so the citation is consistent (resolved per _synthesis/citation-corrections-2026-07-16.md)

interlocutors.name: Makransky & Lilleholt (2018) — ped-sec-09
interlocutors.role: cited for HMD VR's superiority over computer screens in arousal, engagement, and motivation — the affirmative side of the HMD affordance/distraction tension this review stages

interlocutors.name: Girvan, Cathy (2018)
interlocutors.role: primary external theoretical interlocutor for VE/VR definitions, used to resolve (partially) the HMD-vs-non-HMD affordance-attribution question

interlocutors.name: Prior VRCL reviews — Muhammad Nur Affendy & Ajune Wanis (2019); Zheng et al. (2019); Scavarelli et al. (2021)
interlocutors.role: the three reviews this article positions itself as extending via first-ever PRISMA methodology

tensions.axis: HMD VR's affective/motivational advantage (Makransky & Lilleholt 2018) vs. HMD VR's distraction/poorer-learning cost (Makransky et al. 2019; Parong & Mayer 2021)
tensions.note: The review stages both sides explicitly and resolves the tension only conditionally — outcome depends on goals, setting, and which affordance matters most — rather than adjudicating a winner. This directly instantiates this cluster's own debate axis 1 (more immersion -> more learning <-> immersion adds presence but not learning).

tensions.axis: affordances belong to the environment, not the tool (Girvan 2018 framework) vs. tool choice still moderates outcomes
tensions.note: The review's own two-step move: first neutralizes the HMD-vs-non-HMD debate at the definitional level, then immediately re-admits that empirical outcomes still differ by tool.

tensions.axis: general field optimism (70% positive-or-better outcomes) vs. near-total absence of true-experimental designs (5.8%) and physiological measures (0.7%)
tensions.note: The review's own methodological self-critique: optimism is reported alongside a field-wide reliance on pre-experimental, self-report-heavy designs that cannot strongly support causal optimism.
